text: Massing Studio. From a plot address to explained massing directions.

Early in a project, an architect wants to know what a plot can hold. Answering that means digging through cadastral maps, 3D city data and zoning plans, and then sketching volumes by hand. It is slow, and the rules behind each sketch stay hidden. Massing Studio does this groundwork in minutes. It finds the plot, lists the rules with their sources, and generates massing directions the designer can inspect, adjust and export.
We start with an address. Netherlands. Delft. Van Leeuwenhoekpark 1. The tool finds the official cadastral parcel: plot 3458, almost two thousand square metres.

Next, the zoning limits. Allowed use, building height and buildable area are read from the zoning plan, each with its source. Missing values are flagged as unknown, never quietly filled in. One click proposes suggested values, clearly marked as suggestions.

Now the 3D site model, built from real building data. The dashed box is the envelope: everything the rules allow. Four preset directions: most floor area, most daylight, most greenery, and low development. On the right, the computed numbers and a check against every rule.
The designer stays in control. Dragging the coverage slider reshapes the mass and updates the numbers instantly. Sliders never call the AI. Every number comes from code.

Under Your brief, the designer describes the project in plain words: a ring of pitched-roof apartments around a green courtyard, turned towards the sun. The AI reads the brief, sets the priorities, and flags what is unclear.
Then it proposes one direction, with a name and its trade-offs. The geometry is built and checked by code, so every rule result can be traced.
Finally, export. Pick an option and a view, and save an image, a line drawing, or a PDF report.
The report shows the site, each option with its numbers, and every rule with its status and source.

What works: one address becomes inspectable, explained options within minutes, with every number computed and every rule traced to a source. The limits: zoning is only partly read from the plan, and the gaps are filled with suggestions, not verified rules. The tool only models housing, so here it reports the mixed-use plan as a rule not met. Parcel geometry is indicative, and nothing here is a permit check. Next steps: fuller zoning data and more building types.
